issues: 'this is the place where Aṅgulimāla lived' → 捨邪之處 'where Aṅgulimāla abandoned his wicked ways' (Mizutani: 邪心を捨てた所) | 'Therefore, within the old palace city' → 故宮城內 'within the old palace city' (故 = old, not 'therefore') | 'Elder Anāthapiṇḍada (善施長者)' → 善施 = Sudatta | 'surrendered his life' → 歸命 'took refuge'
en_revised: The country of Śrāvastī (室羅伐悉底國) is over 6,000 li in circuit. The capital city is desolate and ruined, and its boundaries are not clearly defined. The old foundations of the palace city are over 20 li in circuit; although it is largely ruined and overgrown, there are still inhabitants. The grain crops are abundant, and the climate is temperate. The customs are simple and honest, and the people are devoted to learning and fond of performing meritorious deeds. There are several hundred saṃghārāmas, most of which are in ruins, and the number of monks is small; they study the Sammatiya school (正量部). There are one hundred deva temples, and non-Buddhists are very numerous. This was the capital city governed by King Prasenajit (鉢邏犀那恃多王) during the time the Tathāgata was in the world. Within the old palace city, there are old foundations which are the remaining traces of the palace of King Prasenajit (勝軍王). Not far to the east, there is an old foundation upon which a small stūpa is built; this was the Great Dharma Hall that King Prasenajit built for the Tathāgata in the past. Not far from the side of the Dharma Hall, there is a stūpa on an old foundation; this is the site of the nunnery (精舍) of the Buddha’s maternal aunt, Mahāprajāpatī (鉢邏闍鉢底), which was established by King Prasenajit. To the east of this stūpa is the old residence of Sudatta (蘇達多). Beside the residence of the Elder Sudatta (善施長者) is a large stūpa; this is the place where Aṅgulimāla (鴦窶利摩羅) abandoned his wicked ways. Aṅgulimāla was a violent man of Śrāvastī. He harmed living beings and terrorized the city and the country, killing people to take their fingers to make a garland for his head. He was about to kill his mother to complete the count of fingers. The World-Honored One, out of compassion, set out to guide and transform him. Seeing the World-Honored One from afar, he secretly rejoiced and said, "I shall now certainly be reborn in heaven." "My former teacher gave me instructions, and his final words were these: 'If one harms a Buddha and kills his mother, he shall be reborn in the Brahma Heaven.'" He said to his mother, "Old lady, stay here for now; I must first kill that great śramaṇa." He immediately took up his sword and went to intercept the World-Honored One. The Tathāgata then retreated at a slow pace, yet the wicked Aṅgulimāla (指鬘) could not catch up even though he ran fast. The World-Honored One said to him, "Why do you cling to such ignoble intentions, abandoning the root of goodness and stirring up the source of evil?" At that time, Aṅgulimāla heard this instruction and realized that his actions were wrong; he then took refuge, sought to enter the Dharma, practiced with diligence and without sloth, and attained the fruit of an Arhat.

en_revised: Five or six li to the south of the city is the Jetavana (逝多林), which is the Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma (給孤獨園). The minister Sudatta (善施) of King Prasenajit (勝軍王) built a vihāra (精舍) for the Buddha; it was formerly a monastery (saṃghārāma), but now it lies in ruins. To the left and right of the east gate stand stone pillars over seventy feet high; the left pillar is topped with a carved wheel, and the right pillar is surmounted by the figure of a bull, both of which were erected by King Aśoka (無憂王). The buildings have collapsed, leaving only the old foundations, save for a single brick chamber that stands alone and imposing, within which is an image of the Buddha. Formerly, after the Tathāgata had ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, King Prasenajit heard that King Udayana (出愛王) had carved a sandalwood image of the Buddha, and he thereupon had this image made. The Elder Sudatta was benevolent and intelligent; he was able to distribute what he had accumulated, helping the needy and relieving the poor, and showing compassion to the orphaned and the elderly. People of the time praised his virtues and called him Anāthapiṇḍada (給孤獨, "the giver to the lonely and solitary"). Having heard of the Buddha’s merits, he developed a deep sense of respect and wished to build a vihāra, inviting the Buddha to descend and visit. The World-Honored One commanded Śāriputra to accompany him to survey the land, and they found that only the garden of Prince Jeta (逝多) was high and dry. He immediately went to the prince and explained his intentions in full. The prince said in jest, "If you cover it with gold, I will sell it." Upon hearing this, Sudatta’s heart was filled with joy; he immediately brought out his hidden gold and covered the ground as he had promised. There was a small portion left uncovered, which the prince asked to keep, saying, "The Buddha is truly a fertile field; it is fitting to plant good seeds." Thereupon, on the vacant land, they built the vihāra. The World-Honored One went there and said to Ānanda, "The garden ground was purchased by Sudatta (善施), and the trees were donated by Jeta (逝多); the two men, being of one mind, have together established this meritorious work. From now on, this place shall be called the Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍikārāma (逝多林給孤獨園)."  To the northeast of the Anāthapiṇḍikārāma is a stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata washed a sick bhikṣu. Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the world, there was a sick bhikṣu who, enduring suffering, lived alone. The World-Honored One saw him and asked, "What is your suffering? Why do you live alone?" He replied, "My nature is lazy and slothful, and I cannot bear to look after the sick; therefore, I am now afflicted with illness, and there is no one to attend to me." At that time, the Tathāgata, feeling compassion, said to him, "Good man, I will now look after you." He stroked him with his hand, and his illness and suffering were all healed. He helped him out of the room, changed his bedding, personally washed him, and put new clothes on him. The Buddha said to the bhikṣu, "You should be diligent yourself." Hearing this instruction, he felt gratitude, and his heart was joyful and his body at ease.  To the northwest of the Anāthapiṇḍikārāma is a small stūpa, which is the place where Maudgalyāyanaputra (沒特伽羅子) exerted his supernatural power to lift Śāriputra’s (舍利子) robe and belt, but could not move them. Formerly, when the Buddha was at Lake Anavatapta (無熱惱池), humans and devas had all gathered, but only Śāriputra did not arrive at the assembly in time. The Buddha ordered Maudgalyāyana to go and summon him to join the assembly. Maudgalyāyana accepted the command and went; Śāriputra was mending his dharma-robe. Maudgalyāyana said, "The World-Honored One is now at Lake Anavatapta and has ordered me to summon you." Śāriputra (舍利子) said, "Wait a moment; I must finish mending this, and then I will go with you." Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅) said, "If you do not go quickly, I shall use my supernatural power to lift your stone chamber and take it to the great assembly." Śāriputra then untied his robe and belt, placed them on the ground, and said, "If you can lift this belt, my body might move." At that time, Maudgalyāyana exerted his great supernatural power, but he could not lift the belt; instead, the earth shook. He then used his supernatural foot-power to return to the place of the Buddha, where he saw that Śāriputra was already seated in the assembly. Maudgalyāyana bowed his head and sighed, saying, "Only now do I know that the power of supernatural abilities is not equal to the power of wisdom."  Not far from the side of the stupa (窣堵波) where the belt was lifted, there is a well. When the Tathāgata (如來) was in the world, water was drawn from it for the Buddha’s use. Beside it is a stupa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which contains the relics of the Tathāgata. The sites of his walking meditation and the places where he preached the Dharma are all marked with banners and have had stupas built upon them. Deities and spirits stand guard, and miraculous signs appear from time to time; sometimes celestial music is played, and at other times divine incense is smelled. These auspicious blessings are difficult to describe in full.  Not far behind the monastery (伽藍) is the place where the non-Buddhist ascetics (外道梵志) murdered a courtesan to slander the Buddha. The Tathāgata possesses the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and omniscience; he is revered by humans and devas, and honored by sages and worthies. At that time, the various non-Buddhists consulted together, saying, "We should employ deceit and slander him in the midst of the crowd." They then enticed and hired a courtesan, pretending she was coming to listen to the Dharma, and once this was known to the public, they secretly murdered her, buried her corpse beside a tree, and lodged a complaint with the king. The king ordered a search, and her body was discovered in the Jetavana (逝多園). At that time, the non-Buddhists loudly proclaimed: "The great śramaṇa Gautama (喬答摩) constantly praises precepts and patience; yet now he has had illicit relations with this woman and murdered her to silence her. Having both fornicated and murdered, where are his precepts and where is his patience?" The devas in the sky followed their voices and proclaimed: "The wicked non-Buddhists have made this slander."  More than one hundred paces to the east of the monastery (伽藍) is a large, deep pit; this is the place where Devadatta (提婆達多), intending to harm the Buddha with poison, fell alive into hell. Devadatta was the son of King Droṇodana (斛飯王). He practiced diligently for twelve years and had already memorized the eighty thousand sections of the Dharma-store. Later, for the sake of profit, he sought to learn supernatural powers and associated with evil friends, consulting with them and saying: "My physical marks are thirty, not much less than the Buddha's; surrounded by the great assembly, how am I different from the Tathāgata?" Having thought this, he proceeded to cause a schism in the Sangha. Śāriputra (舍利子) and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子), following the Buddha’s instructions and relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power, preached the Dharma and offered exhortations, and the Sangha was restored to harmony. Devadatta did not relinquish his evil intentions; he placed a deadly poison under his fingernails, intending to harm the Buddha while performing an act of homage. As he was carrying out this plot, coming from afar and arriving at this spot, the earth suddenly split open, and he fell alive into hell. To the south of this, there is another large pit where the bhikṣu Kokālika (瞿伽梨) fell alive into hell for slandering the Tathāgata. More than eight hundred paces to the south of the pit of Kokālika, there is a large, deep pit, which is the place where the Brahmin woman Ciñcā (戰遮) fell alive into hell for slandering the Tathāgata.  When the Buddha was preaching the essential Dharma to humans and devas, a disciple of an externalist sect saw from afar the great assembly paying homage to the World-Honored One and thought to herself, "I must humiliate Gautama today and ruin his good reputation, so that my own teacher may alone possess a fragrant name." She then concealed a wooden basin tied to her belly and went to the Jetavana (給孤獨園), where she cried out in a loud voice before the great assembly, "This preacher has had illicit relations with me, and the child in my womb is of the Śākya clan." Those with wrong views all believed her, while those who were steadfast and firm knew it was a slanderous accusation.  At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, wishing to dispel the doubt, transformed himself into a white mouse and gnawed through the cord holding the basin. The sound of the cord snapping startled the great assembly, and all who saw and heard it felt a deep sense of joy. One person in the assembly stood up, held the wooden basin, and showed it to the woman, saying, "Is this your child?" At that moment, the earth split open of its own accord, and she fell in, her whole body sinking into the Avīci hell to suffer the full consequences of her actions.  These three pits are bottomless; during the heavy rains of autumn and summer, when ditches and pools overflow, no water ever remains in these deep hollows. Sixty or seventy paces to the east of the monastery, there is a vihāra (精舍) more than sixty feet high, in which there is an image of the Buddha seated facing east. In the past, the Tathāgata debated with various heretics here. To the east of this is a deva temple, equal in size to the vihāra (精舍). When the sun rises and sheds its light, the shadow of the deva temple does not cover the vihāra; when the sun is about to set, the shadow of the vihāra covers the deva temple. Three or four *li* to the east of the Shadow-covering Vihāra (影覆精舍), there is a stūpa, which is the place where the Venerable Śāriputra debated with the heretics.  Initially, the elder Sudatta (善施長者) purchased the garden of Prince Jeta (逝多太子) and wished to build a vihāra for the Tathāgata. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra accompanied the elder to survey the site. The teachers of the six heretical schools sought to compete in supernatural powers, but Śāriputra converted them according to the circumstances and subdued them in response to their challenges. Beside this, in front of the vihāra, a stūpa was built; it was here that the Tathāgata defeated the various heretics and also accepted the invitation of Mother Viśākhā (毘舍佉母).  To the south of the stūpa where he accepted the invitation is the place where King Virūḍhaka (毘盧釋迦王) mobilized his army to slaughter the Śākya clan, and where he saw the Buddha and turned his army back. After King Virūḍhaka ascended the throne, he pursued his resentment over a previous humiliation, mobilized his army, and moved his great host. Once the deployment was complete and the orders were issued, he set out. At that time, a bhikṣu heard of this and reported it to the Buddha. The World-Honored One then sat beneath a withered tree. King Virūḍhaka saw the World-Honored One from afar, dismounted to pay his respects, and standing to the side, said, "Lush trees are spreading and thick; why do you not sit beneath them? Why do you dwell by a withered, rotten stump?" The World-Honored One replied, "One's kinsmen are like the branches and leaves. When the branches and leaves are in danger, where is the shade?" The King said, "The World-Honored One is doing this for his kinsmen; I may turn my chariot back." Thereupon, seeing the Holy One, he was moved with emotion, turned his army back, and returned to his country. Beside the place where the army turned back, there is a stūpa, which is the place where the Śākya women were slaughtered. When King Virūḍhaka had conquered the Śākyas, he selected five hundred women to fill his palace. The Śākya women were resentful and angry, and spoke insolent words of complaint, reviling the King, saying, "You are the son of a domestic servant." When the King heard this, he became enraged and ordered them to be slaughtered. The executioners obeyed the King’s command, severed their hands and feet, and threw them into a pit. At that time, the Śākya women, enduring their suffering, called upon the Buddha. The World-Honored One, with his holy insight, perceived their bitter agony and commanded the bhikṣus to gather their robes and go there to preach the subtle Dharma to the Śākya women, namely, that they were bound by the five desires, wandering through the three evil paths, suffering the separation of loved ones, and that birth and death are long and far-reaching. When the Śākya women heard the Buddha’s instruction, they distanced themselves from dust and removed their stains, attained the pure Dharma-eye, and at the same time passed away, all being reborn in the heavens. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra transformed himself into a brāhmaṇa, collected their remains, and cremated them; later generations have marked the spot. Not far from the stūpa of the slaughtered Śākyas, there is a large dried-up pond, which is the place where King Virūḍhaka sank into hell. After the World-Honored One had observed the Śākya women, he returned to the Jetavana (逝多林給孤獨園) and told the bhikṣus, "Seven days from now, King Virūḍhaka will be consumed by fire." When the King heard the Buddha’s prophecy, he was filled with great fear and trepidation. When the seventh day arrived, he was peaceful and in no danger. The king, feeling jubilant, ordered the palace maidens to go to the riverside to enjoy themselves with music and wine. Still fearing that a fire might break out, he rowed upon the clear currents and drifted along with the waves. Suddenly, a blazing fire erupted, consuming the light boat; the king’s body fell, and he entered the Avīci Hell to undergo all manner of suffering.

issues: 'all marked by trees and designated by stūpas' → 並樹封記，建窣堵波 'markers have been set up and stūpas built' (樹 = to set up)
en_revised: Three or four li to the northwest of the monastery, one reaches the Wood of Regained Sight (Andhavana). There are traces of the Tathāgata’s walking meditation and places where various sages practiced concentration, all marked by commemorative signs, with stūpas built. In the past, there was a band of five hundred bandits in this country who ran amok in the villages and acted lawlessly throughout the cities and states. King Prasenajit (勝軍王) captured them, gouged out their eyes, and abandoned them in the deep forest. The bandits, tormented by suffering, cried out in supplication to the Buddha. At that time, the Tathāgata was in the Jetavana Monastery (逝多精舍); hearing their cries of grief, he felt great compassion, and a gentle, cooling breeze blew medicinal herbs from the Snow Mountains into their eyes, whereupon their sight was immediately restored. Upon seeing the World-Honored One standing before them, they conceived the resolve for enlightenment, bowed in joyful worship, and departed after casting down their staves, which then took root there.

en_revised: From here, traveling southeast for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Kapilavastu (劫比羅伐窣堵國). The country of Kapilavastu is over four thousand *li* in circuit. There are more than ten empty cities, which are extremely desolate and overgrown. The royal city is in ruins, and its exact circuit is unknown. The inner palace city is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit; it was built of piled bricks, and its foundations remain steep and solid. Having been desolate for a long time, the inhabited villages are sparse and wide apart. There is no great monarch; each city has its own ruler. The land is fertile and rich, and crops are sown in their proper seasons. The climate is regular, and the customs are harmonious and pleasant. There are more than a thousand old foundations of *saṃghārāmas*. Beside the palace city, there is one *saṃghārāma* with more than three thousand monks who study the teachings of the Sammatiya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are two temples to the gods; followers of different paths live intermixed.  Inside the palace city are the old foundations of the main hall of King Śuddhodana (淨飯王). A vihāra (精舍) has been built upon it, containing a statue of the king. Not far to its side are the old foundations of the bedchamber of Queen Mahāmāyā (摩訶摩耶夫人). A vihāra has been built upon it, containing a statue of the queen. The vihāra beside it marks the place where the Bodhisattva Śākya descended into his mother’s womb, and inside is a representation of the Bodhisattva’s descent. The Sthavira school holds that the Bodhisattva descended into his mother’s womb on the night of the thirtieth day of the month of Uttarāṣāḍhā, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the fifth month here; the various other schools hold that he descended into his mother’s womb on the night of the twenty-third day of that month, which corresponds to the eighth day of the fifth month here. To the northeast of the place where the Bodhisattva descended, there is a *stūpa* marking the place where the sage Asita examined the prince. On the day the Bodhisattva was born, auspicious signs converged. At that time, King Śuddhodana (淨飯王) summoned the physiognomists and said to them, "This child has been born; what is his fortune, good or evil? You must examine him thoroughly and speak clearly in your reply." They said, "According to the records of the ancient sages and examining the auspicious omens, if he remains in household life, he will become a Cakravartin king; if he renounces the household, he will attain Samyak-saṃbuddha." At that time, the sage Asita (阿私多仙) arrived from afar and knocked at the gate to request an audience. The King was very joyful, personally welcomed and paid homage to him, and invited him to take a precious seat, saying, "I did not expect the Great Sage to visit today." The sage said, "While I was dwelling in peace and sitting at ease in the heavenly palace, I suddenly saw hosts of devas dancing. I then asked them, 'Why are you so extremely joyful?' They replied, 'Great Sage, you should know that the first lady of King Śuddhodana of the Śākya clan in Jambudvīpa has now given birth to a prince, who shall realize Samyak-saṃbodhi and perfectly illuminate all-encompassing wisdom.' Having heard these words, I came to pay my respects. What I lament is my decrepit old age, which will not allow me to encounter his holy transformation."  At the south gate of the city is a *stūpa* marking the place where the Prince competed in feats of strength with the other Śākyas and threw an elephant. The Prince was highly skilled in many arts, standing alone and peerless. King Śuddhodana, feeling joyful, was about to return, and a servant was driving an elephant, just about to exit the city. Devadatta (提婆達多), who had always prided himself on his great strength, came in from the outside and asked the driver, "You have prepared this elephant; who is going to ride it?" He replied, "The Prince is about to return, so I am going to serve as his driver." Devadatta, in a fit of anger, pulled the elephant, struck its forehead, and kicked its chest, causing it to fall dead and block the road, obstructing the path so that no one could move it, and the crowds were jammed. Nanda arrived later and asked, "Who killed this elephant?" They replied, "Devadatta." He immediately dragged it aside to clear the road. The Prince arrived and also asked, "Who did this evil deed and killed this elephant?" They replied, "Devadatta killed it to block the gate, and Nanda dragged it to open the path." The Prince then lifted the elephant and threw it high, over the city moat. Where the elephant fell to the ground, it formed a large, deep pit, which local tradition calls the Pit of the Fallen Elephant. In a vihāra (精舍) beside it, a statue of the Prince has been made. Beside that is another vihāra, which was the bedchamber of the Prince’s consort; inside are statues of Yaśodharā and Rāhula. In the vihāra beside the palace, a statue is made in the posture of receiving instruction; this is the original site of the Prince’s schoolroom. At the southeast corner of the city is a vihāra containing a statue of the Prince riding a white horse through the air, marking the spot where he leaped over the city wall. Outside the four gates of the city, there is a vihāra at each, containing statues of an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a *śramaṇa* (沙門). These represent the Prince’s excursions, where, upon seeing these signs, his concern deepened, he felt a profound weariness with the mundane world, became enlightened at these sights, and ordered his servant to turn the carriage back.

issues: 'The devas, wishing to warn the hearts of men, gathered the remains and buried them' → 天警人心，收骸瘞葬 'Heaven stirred men's hearts, and they gathered the remains and buried them' | note: 數百千窣堵波 'several hundred thousand' may also be read 'hundreds and thousands' (Beal); DM's reading kept
en_revised: More than forty li to the northeast of the city, there is a stūpa marking the place where the Prince sat in the shade of a tree, watched the plowing of the fields, and practiced meditation, thereby attaining freedom from desire. When King Śuddhodana (淨飯王) saw the Prince sitting in the shade of the tree, having entered into tranquil meditation, while the sunlight shone brightly yet the shadow of the tree did not move, he knew in his heart that the Prince was spiritually holy, and he cherished and respected him all the more.  To the northwest of the great city, there are several hundred thousand stūpas; these are the places where the Śākya clan were slaughtered. After King Virūḍhaka (毘盧釋迦王) had conquered the Śākyas, he took their kin captive, obtaining ninety-nine million nine hundred thousand people, all of whom he put to death. The piled-up corpses were like a thicket, and the flowing blood formed a pond. Heaven stirred the hearts of men, and they gathered the remains and buried them.  To the southwest of the place where the Śākyas were slaughtered, there are four small stūpas; these are the places where four Śākya men resisted the army. Originally, when King Prasenajit (勝軍王) ascended the throne, he sought a marriage alliance with the Śākyas. The Śākyas, despising him as not being of their own kind, deceitfully gave him the daughter of a servant, yet they betrothed her with great ceremony. King Prasenajit established her as his principal queen, and she gave birth to a son, who was King Virūḍhaka.  When Virūḍhaka wished to go to his maternal uncles to request instruction and pursue his studies, he arrived south of this city and, seeing a new lecture hall, stopped his carriage to rest inside. When the Śākyas heard of this, they drove him out, cursing him: "You base-born slave, how dare you occupy this hall! This hall was built by the Śākyas, intended for the Buddha to reside in." After Virūḍhaka ascended the throne, he sought to avenge this former humiliation, so he raised an army and marched to this place to encamp his troops. Four members of the Śākya clan, who were personally plowing the fields, immediately resisted them; the invading army retreated and dispersed, and the four men then entered the city. Their clansmen, believing that as descendants of a Universal Monarch (cakravartin) and sons of the Dharma King, they should not have dared to commit acts of violence or heartlessly kill others, felt they had disgraced the clan; consequently, they severed ties with them and sent them into distant exile. After the four men were expelled, they fled north to the Snow Mountains; one became the king of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國), one the king of Bāmīyān (梵衍那國), one the king of Himatala (呬摩呾羅國), and one the king of Śami (商彌國). Their dynasties passed down the throne for generations, and their lineage remained unbroken.

issues: 'at the place of the parinirvāṇa' → 涅疊般那地 'the cremation ground' (Mizutani: 旧に闍維と云う)
en_revised: Southeast of the stupa where the prince had his hair shaved, after traveling one hundred and eighty or ninety li through a wilderness, one reaches the Nyagrodha grove (尼拘盧陀林), where there is a stupa over thirty feet high. In the past, when the Tathāgata attained parinirvāṇa and the relics had already been divided, the various Brahmins who had obtained none gathered the remaining ashes and charcoal at the cremation ground (涅疊般那), brought them to their own country, and built this sacred foundation to perform offerings. From that time onward, miraculous signs have occurred in succession, and those suffering from illnesses who pray here are often healed. Beside the Ash and Charcoal Stupa (灰炭窣堵波), within an old monastery, there are sites marking where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation. Around this old monastery are several hundred stupas. One large one among them was built by King Aśoka (無憂王); although its lofty base has collapsed, it is over one hundred feet high. From here, traveling northeast through a great forest, the road is difficult and dangerous; mountain oxen, wild elephants, bands of robbers, and hunters lie in wait for travelers, and the harm they cause is incessant.

issues: 'A hare arrived later and, enduring fatigue and suffering, helped the deer. When their strength was exhausted, they drowned' → 蹇兔後至，忍疲苦而濟之。筋力既竭，溺水而死: a lame hare came last and the deer, enduring its exhaustion, rescued it; then the deer drowned (Mizutani: 跛の兎が最後にやって来た; consistent with 即昔後渡蹇兔 later in the passage) | 'to the place of nirvana (涅疊般那)' → 'the cremation ground' | *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) → 精舍 is simply 'vihāra'; the specific term is not in the Chinese
en_revised: Three or four *li* to the northwest of the city, one crosses the Ajitavatī River. Not far from the western bank, one arrives at the Sāla grove (Skt. *sāla*). The trees resemble the oak, but their bark is greenish-white and their leaves are very glossy and smooth. Four trees are especially tall; this is the place where the Tathāgata attained extinction. In the large brick vihāra (精舍) there is an image of the Tathāgata in *nirvāṇa*, lying with his head to the north. Beside it is a *stūpa* built by King Aśoka; although the base has collapsed and sunken, it is still over two hundred feet high. In front of it stands a stone pillar to record the event of the Tathāgata’s extinction; although there is an inscription, it does not record the day or month. I have heard from various ancient records that the Buddha entered *parinirvāṇa* at the age of eighty on the fifteenth day of the latter half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the third month here. The Sarvāstivāda school, however, holds that the Buddha entered *parinirvāṇa* on the eighth day of the latter half of the month of Kārttika, which corresponds to the eighth day of the ninth month here. Since the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, the various schools have held differing opinions: some say more than 1,200 years have passed, some say more than 1,300 years, some say more than 1,500 years, and others say more than 900 but less than 1,000 years. Not far from the side of the vihāra is a *stūpa*; this is the place where, when the Tathāgata was practicing the Bodhisattva path, he was the king of a flock of pheasants and saved them from a fire. Formerly, there was a great, dense forest in this place, where feathered and furred creatures lived in nests and burrows. A sudden wind arose from all directions, and the fierce flames spread rapidly. At that time, there was a pheasant who, feeling compassion, soaked its wings in the clear stream, flew into the air, and shook the water to sprinkle the flames. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra (天帝釋) looked down and said, "Why do you persist in such folly, tiring your wings in vain? A great fire has just broken out, burning the forest and wilderness; how could your tiny body possibly extinguish it?" The pheasant replied, "Who is it that speaks?" He said, "I am Śakra Devānām Indra." The pheasant replied, "Today, the Heavenly Emperor possesses great merit and power, and there is no desire that he cannot fulfill. To relieve disasters and rescue those in distress should be as easy as looking at one's own palm; yet you instead question my lack of success—where does the blame truly lie? The fierce fire is currently raging; say no more!" The pheasant then exerted itself and flew off again, heading toward the flowing water. The Heavenly Emperor then scooped up water with his hands and sprinkled it over the forest; the fire was extinguished and the smoke vanished, and the lives of all creatures were preserved. Therefore, it is now called the Fire-fighting Stūpa.  Not far from the side of the place where the pheasant fought the fire, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the Bodhisattva path, saved lives as a deer. In the remote past, there was a great forest here. A fire broke out in the wilderness, and the birds and beasts were driven to desperation, facing the peril of a swift current in front and the hardship of a raging fire behind, such that none escaped drowning or losing their lives. The deer, moved by compassion, positioned its body across the current, its skin pierced and bones broken, exerting itself to rescue the drowning. A lame hare arrived last, and the deer, enduring its fatigue and pain, rescued it as well. When its strength was exhausted, the deer drowned and died. The devas collected its remains and erected a stūpa.  Not far to the west of the place where the deer rescued the drowning is a stūpa, which marks the spot where Subhadra (蘇跋陀羅) entered into final extinction. Subhadra (translated as "Good Sage" [善賢]) was originally a teacher of the Brahmins. He was one hundred and twenty years old, an elder of great wisdom. Hearing that the Buddha was about to enter extinction, he arrived between the twin trees and asked Ānanda, "The Buddha, the World-Honored One, is about to enter extinction. I have doubts and hesitations, and I wish to ask him questions." Ānanda said, "The Buddha is about to enter nirvāṇa; please do not disturb him." He replied, "I have heard that it is difficult to encounter a Buddha in the world and difficult to hear the true Dharma. I have deep doubts and fear that I will have no one to ask." Subhadra (蘇跋陀羅) then entered and first asked the Buddha, "There are various other groups who call themselves teachers, each with different doctrines, handing down instructions to guide the laity. Can Gautama (喬答摩) know them all?" The Buddha said, "I have thoroughly investigated them all," and then he expounded them for him. Having heard this, Subhadra’s heart was purified and he gained faith and understanding; he sought to enter the Dharma and receive the full ordination. The Tathāgata said to him, "Are you capable of this? For those of other paths and different schools who practice the holy life, they must be tested for four years. One observes their conduct and examines their nature; if their deportment is tranquil and their speech is truthful, then they may practice the holy life in my Dharma. It depends on the person's practice; what difficulty is there in this!" Subhadra said, "The World-Honored One is compassionate and merciful, saving all without partiality. As for the four-year probationary period, the three karmas will then be in accord." The Buddha said, "I have already said it: it depends on the person's practice!" Thereupon, Subhadra renounced the household life and immediately received the full ordination, diligently and energetically practicing, with body and mind courageous. Soon after, he had no more doubts about the Dharma and personally attained realization. Before the night was far spent, he attained the fruit of an arhat; all his outflows were exhausted, and the holy life was established. Unable to bear seeing the Buddha enter mahānirvāṇa, he entered the samādhi of the fire element amidst the assembly, manifested supernatural powers, and entered nirvana first. He was the Tathāgata’s final disciple, yet he attained extinction first; this is the one who in the past was the hare that crossed the river last. Beside the place where Subhadra (善賢) attained extinction, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the Vajra-holder (執金剛) fell to the ground. The Great Compassionate World-Honored One, having appeared to benefit beings according to their capacities and having completed his work of transformation, entered the joy of extinction, lying down with his head to the north between the twin trees. When the Vajra-holding deity, the Guhyapāda Malla (密迹力士), saw the Buddha enter extinction, he cried out in bitter grief: "The Tathāgata has forsaken me and entered mahānirvāṇa; I have no refuge and no protection; the poisoned arrow has struck deep, and the fire of sorrow burns fiercely!" He cast aside his vajra-club and fell to the ground in a swoon. After a long time he rose again, and in his sorrow and longing, they said to one another: "In the great ocean of birth and death, who shall serve as our boat and oar? In the long night of ignorance, who shall be our lamp and torch?" Beside the place where the Vajra-holder fell to the ground, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the Tathāgata was venerated for seven days after his extinction. When the Tathāgata was about to enter extinction, light shone everywhere, and humans and devas all gathered; there was none who did not feel sorrow, and they said to one another: "The Great Awakened World-Honored One is now about to enter extinction; the merit of sentient beings is exhausted, and the world is without a refuge." The Tathāgata lay on his right side on a lion-couch and told the great assembly: "Do not say that the Tathāgata has entered final extinction; his Dharma-body is eternally abiding and free from all change. You should abandon sloth and seek liberation quickly." The bhikṣus sobbed and lamented. At that time, Aniruddha (阿泥𢫫陀) said to the bhikṣus, "Stop, stop, do not grieve! The devas will mock and wonder at you." When the Malla (末羅) assembly had finished their offerings and wished to lift the golden coffin to proceed to the cremation ground (涅疊般那), Aniruddha said, "Wait! The devas wish to remain for seven days to make offerings." Thereupon, the host of devas, holding wondrous heavenly flowers, traveled through the void, praising the holy virtues, each exhausting their sincere hearts to join in making offerings. Beside where the coffin rested is a stūpa, which is the place where Lady Mahāmāyā (摩訶摩耶夫人) wept for the Buddha. After the Tathāgata had entered extinction and the encoffining was completed, Aniruddha ascended to the heavenly palace and told Lady Māyā, "The Great Holy Dharma King has now entered extinction." Upon hearing this, Māyā choked with grief and fainted; then, together with the host of devas, she arrived between the twin trees. Seeing the saṃghāṭī (僧伽胝), the bowl, and the khakkhara (錫杖), she stroked them and wailed, losing consciousness and then reviving, saying, "The merit of humans and devas is exhausted; the eye of the world is extinguished! Now these objects are empty and without an owner." By the holy power of the Tathāgata, the golden coffin opened of itself, emitted light, and he sat up with palms joined to comfort his compassionate mother: "You have come from afar to descend! All conditioned things are by nature thus; I pray you do not grieve deeply." Ānanda (阿難), holding back his sorrow, requested of the Buddha, "If future generations ask me, how shall I respond?" [He] said: "The Buddha had already entered nirvāṇa, [when] his compassionate mother Māyā descended from the heavenly palace to the space between the twin trees. For the sake of unfilial sentient beings, the Tathāgata rose from the golden coffin, joined his palms, and preached the Dharma."

issues: 'he has extinguished the bright guide of the world' → 滅世間明導 'the bright guide of the world has been extinguished [here]' (the Tathāgata is not the agent)
en_revised: Crossing the river more than three hundred paces to the north of the city, there is a stupa, which is the place where the Tathāgata (如來) was cremated. The ground is now yellow and black, the soil mixed with ash and charcoal; if one requests with utmost sincerity, one may obtain relics. When the Tathāgata entered into extinction, humans and devas were moved by grief; they made a coffin of the seven treasures and wrapped his body in a thousand layers of fine cotton, offered incense and flowers, and set up banners and canopies. The Malla (末羅) people then bore the hearse in a procession, with guides in front and followers behind, crossing the Gold River to the north, where they filled it with fragrant oil, piled up much scented wood, and set it ablaze. Two layers of the cotton did not burn: one that was closest to the body and one that covered the outermost layer. In order to distribute the relics for all sentient beings, only the hair and nails remained intact and undamaged. Beside the place of cremation is a stupa, marking the spot where the Tathāgata revealed his two feet to Mahākāśyapa (大迦葉波). When the Tathāgata’s golden coffin had been lowered and the fragrant wood piled up, the fire would not ignite, and the assembly was filled with alarm. Aniruddha (阿泥𢫫陀) said, "We must wait for Kāśyapa." At that time, Mahākāśyapa, with five hundred disciples, came from the mountain forests and arrived at the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城). He asked Ānanda, "Can the body of the World-Honored One still be seen?" Ānanda replied, "It is wrapped in a thousand layers of fine cotton, enclosed in heavy coffins, and the fragrant wood has already been piled up; the cremation is about to take place." At that moment, the Buddha, from within the coffin, revealed his two feet; upon the wheel-marks, a strange color was visible. He asked Ānanda, "Why is there this color?" He replied, "When the Buddha first entered parinirvāṇa, humans and devas were overcome with grief, and the tears of the multitude splashed and stained it, causing this strange color." Kāśyapa paid homage, circumambulated, and offered praises; the fragrant wood ignited spontaneously, and a great fire blazed fiercely. Thus, when the Tathāgata entered extinction, he emerged from the coffin three times: first, he extended his arm to ask Ānanda about the path; next, he sat up to preach the Dharma for his mother; finally, he revealed his two feet to show them to Mahākāśyapa. Beside the place where he revealed his feet is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is the site where the eight kings divided the relics. In front of it, a stone pillar was erected, inscribed with an account of the event. After the Buddha had entered nirvāṇa and the cremation was completed, the kings of eight countries arrived with their fourfold armies and dispatched a straightforward Brahmin to say to the Mallas of Kuśinagara (拘尸力士), "The Teacher of gods and men has entered extinction in this country; therefore, we have come from afar to request a share of the relics." The Mallas replied, "The Tathāgata descended in his majesty to this lower realm; here the bright guide of the world has been extinguished and we have lost the compassionate father of all living beings. The relics of the Tathāgata should naturally be worshipped by us alone; you have wearied yourselves on the road in vain, for you shall never obtain them." At that time, the various great kings requested them with humble words, but since they were not granted, they said again, "If polite requests are not followed, the might of our armies is not far off." The straightforward Brahmin spoke aloud, "Reflect! The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One patiently cultivated merit and goodness throughout vast kalpas, as I presume you have all heard; it is not appropriate for you now to seek to oppress one another. Since the relics are here, they should be divided into eight equal portions so that each may receive them for worship; why go so far as to raise troops?" The Mallas followed his words and immediately measured the relics, intending to divide them into eight portions. Śakra (帝釋) said to the kings, "The heavens should have a share; do not rely on force to compete." The Nāga kings Anavatapta (阿那婆答多), Mucilinda (文隣), and Elāpattra (醫那鉢呾羅) also proposed, "Do not exclude us. If it comes to force, the masses are no match for us." The straightforward Brahmin said, "Do not clamor and contend; it is proper to divide them together." He immediately made three portions: first for the devas, second for the Nāga host, and third to remain among humans, which the eight kingdoms then subdivided. The devas, Nāgas, and human kings were all moved to sorrow.

issues: note: 攝衣即語 rendered 'adjusted his robes and spoke'; Mizutani renders 'was about to leave' (立ち去ろうとした, perhaps a variant 即去), which fits the brahmin's 今何無言; CBETA text kept
'Sthavira-Saṃmitīya school' → 小乘正量部 'Sammatiya school of the Lesser Vehicle'; no Sthavira in the Chinese
en_revised: The country of Vārāṇasī (婆羅痆斯國) is over four thousand li in circumference. The capital city of the country borders the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) River to the west; it is eighteen or nineteen li long and five or six li wide. The houses are arranged like the teeth of a comb, the inhabitants are prosperous, families possess vast wealth, and their rooms are filled with rare goods. The people are gentle and respectful by nature, and the customs value diligent study; many believe in non-Buddhist paths, and few respect the Buddha-dharma. The climate is temperate, cereal crops are abundant, fruit trees grow luxuriantly, and the grasses are lush and thick. There are more than thirty saṃghārāmas with over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Sammatiya school (正量部) of the Lesser Vehicle. There are over one hundred deva temples with more than ten thousand followers of other paths, most of whom worship Maheśvara; some cut their hair, others wear it in a topknot, they go naked without clothing and smear their bodies with ash, diligently practicing austerities to seek liberation from birth and death. Within the great city are twenty deva temples with multi-storied terraces and shrines made of carved stone and ornamented wood, shaded by luxuriant forests and encircled by clear streams; there is a brass statue of the deity nearly one hundred feet tall, solemn and majestic as if it were alive.

issues: 'Vārāṇasī River' → 婆羅痆河 = the Varaṇā river (as DM in 07.01.02) | 'temple (mūla-gandha-kuṭī 精舍)' → 'vihāra'
en_revised: Traveling northeast from the Varaṇā River (婆羅痆河) for more than ten li, one arrives at the Deer Park Monastery (Mṛgadāva 鹿野伽藍). The grounds are divided into eight sections, enclosed by a continuous wall, with multi-storied halls and pavilions of exquisite architectural splendor. There are one thousand five hundred monks, all studying the teachings of the Hīnayāna Sāmmitīya school. Within the great enclosure is a vihāra (精舍) over two hundred feet high, topped with a golden *āmra* fruit in relief; it has a stone foundation and steps, with brick niches arranged in tiers surrounding it in hundreds of levels, each containing a golden Buddha image in relief. Inside the vihāra is a brass statue of the Buddha, equal in size to the Tathāgata’s body, in the posture of turning the wheel of the Dharma.

issues: *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) → 精舍 is simply 'vihāra'; the specific term is not in the Chinese
en_revised: To the southwest of the vihāra (精舍) is a stone *stūpa* built by King Aśoka (無憂王); although its foundation has collapsed, it still remains one hundred feet high. In front of it stands a stone pillar, over seventy feet high. The stone is as lustrous as jade and as clear as a mirror; those who pray with sincere devotion may see various images reflected within it, and at times, signs of good and evil are revealed to the observer. This is the place where the Tathāgata, having attained perfect enlightenment, first turned the wheel of the Dharma. Not far to its side is a *stūpa* marking the spot where Ājñātakauṇḍinya (阿若憍陳如) and the others, seeing the Bodhisattva abandon his ascetic practices, ceased to attend upon him and came here to practice meditation by themselves. Beside it is a *stūpa* marking the place where five hundred *pratyekabuddhas* entered *nirvāṇa* together. There are also three *stūpas* marking the sites where the three past Buddhas sat and walked in meditation.

issues: 'Beside the place where the Buddha walked' → 三佛經行側 'beside the walking place of the three Buddhas'
en_revised: Beside the place where the three Buddhas walked, there is a stūpa marking the spot where the Bodhisattva Maitreya (梅呾麗耶) received the prediction of his future Buddhahood. Long ago, when the Tathāgata was on Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa) near the city of Rājagṛha, he told the bhikṣus: "In a future age, when the land of this Jambudvīpa is level and even, and the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, there will be a son of a Brahmin named Maitreya (慈氏), whose body will be of a true golden color, shining with brilliant light. He shall leave his home to attain perfect enlightenment and will widely preach the Dharma for sentient beings in three assemblies. Those whom he saves will all be beings who planted roots of merit under my dispensation. Whether lay or monastic, whether keeping the precepts or violating them, all who harbor deep respect and a single mind toward the Three Jewels will receive his guidance and attain the fruit of liberation. Within these three assemblies of preaching, he will save those who are of my dispensation, and only then will he transform those who are his own karmically connected friends." At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, having heard these words of the Buddha, rose from his seat and said to the Buddha: "I vow that I shall be that Maitreya, the World-Honored One." The Tathāgata replied: "As you have said, you shall attain this fruit. All that has been said above is the method of your teaching and transformation."  To the west of the place where the Bodhisattva Maitreya received his prediction, there is a stūpa marking the spot where the Bodhisattva Śākya (釋迦) received his prediction. During the Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the Buddha Kāśyapa (迦葉波) appeared in the world, turned the wheel of the wonderful Dharma, and opened and transformed sentient beings. He bestowed a prediction upon the Bodhisattva Prabhāpāla (護明), saying: "This Bodhisattva, in a future age when the lifespan of sentient beings is one hundred years, shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni." Not far to the south of the place where the Bodhisattva Śākya (釋迦) received his prediction, there are the traces of the four past Buddhas walking to and fro. The site is over fifty paces long and about seven feet high, built of piled bluestone, and upon it is an image of the Tathāgata in the act of walking. The appearance of the image is extraordinary and solemn; from the top of the uṣṇīṣa (肉髻), hair uniquely emerges, its spiritual features are fully revealed, and its divine intelligence is clearly evidenced. Within its enclosure, sacred traces are truly numerous, with several hundred vihāras (精舍) and stūpas (窣堵波); I have briefly cited two or three, as it would be difficult to describe them all in detail.

issues: 'I am a human with the body of a deer, while you are a deer with the body of a human' → 我人身鹿也，爾鹿身人也 'I am a deer in human body; you are a human in deer's body' — reversed (Mizutani: 人身でありながら鹿…鹿身でありながら人) | 'If heretics or wicked people step lightly upon this stone' → 外道凶人輕蹈此石 'if wicked heretics tread on this stone with contempt'
en_revised: To the west of the monastery enclosure is a clear pond, more than two hundred paces in circumference, where the Tathāgata once bathed. Further west is a large pond, one hundred and eighty paces in circumference, where the Tathāgata once washed his utensils. Further north is a pond, one hundred and fifty paces in circumference, where the Tathāgata once washed his robes. All three of these ponds are inhabited by dragons. Their water is deep and its taste is sweet; it is clear, pure, and bright, and it neither increases nor decreases. If someone with an arrogant mind washes in these ponds, the Kumbhīra (金毘羅) beasts often harm them; if one is deeply respectful, one may draw and use the water without fear. On a large square rock beside the robe-washing pond, there are traces of the Tathāgata’s robes; the patterns are clear and bright, as if carved or engraved, and the faithful often come here to make offerings. If wicked heretics tread contemptuously upon this stone, the dragon king in the pond immediately stirs up wind and rain. Not far from the pond is a stūpa, marking the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the bodhisattva path, was a six-tusked elephant king; a hunter, coveting his tusks, disguised himself in a monk’s robe and lay in wait with a drawn bow, but the elephant king, out of respect for the robe, broke off his tusks and gave them to him. Not far from the place where the tusks were broken is a stūpa, marking the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the bodhisattva path, felt pity for the world’s lack of propriety and manifested as a bird. Together with a monkey and a white elephant, he asked here who had first seen the Nyagrodha (尼拘律) tree. Each recounted their experiences, and they established seniority accordingly. Through this, the influence of the teaching gradually spread, people learned the order of precedence, and both the ordained and the laity took refuge. Not far from its side, in a great forest, there is a stūpa marking the place where the Tathāgata, in the past, while he and Devadatta (提婆達多) were both deer kings, settled a matter. Formerly, in this great forest, there were two herds of deer, each numbering more than five hundred. At that time, the king of this country was hunting in the plains and marshes. The Bodhisattva deer king came forward and petitioned the king, saying: "Your Majesty is hunting across the plains, setting fires and loosing flying arrows. All my followers will lose their lives this morning; in a few days they will rot and stink, serving no purpose as food. I wish to arrange a rotation to deliver one deer each day. Your Majesty will have fresh meat for your meals, and I will prolong our lives for a little while." The king approved his words, turned his carriage around, and returned. The two herds of deer took turns delivering their lives. In Devadatta’s herd, there was a pregnant doe whose turn it was to die; she said to her king, "Although I am due to die, my unborn child’s turn has not yet come." The deer king replied angrily, "Who does not treasure their own life!" The doe sighed and said, "My king is inhumane; death is not far off." She then went to report her emergency to the Bodhisattva deer king. The deer king said, "How sorrowful is the heart of a compassionate mother, whose kindness extends even to her unborn child! I will now take your place." He then went to the king’s gate. People on the road passed the word along, calling out, "That great deer king is now entering the city." The city dwellers and commoners all rushed to watch. When the king heard of it, he thought it was not true. The gatekeeper reported it to the king, and the king then believed it. He said, "Why has the deer king come so suddenly?" The deer said, "There is a doe who is due to die, but her fetus has not yet been born; my heart cannot bear it, so I venture to offer my own body in her stead." Upon hearing this, the king sighed and said, "I am a deer in a human body; you are a human in a deer's body." Thereupon, he released all the deer and no longer required them to forfeit their lives, designating that forest as a sanctuary for the deer; thus, it was called the Forest Given to the Deer (Mr̥gadāva). The name "Deer Park" originated from this.

issues: *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) → 精舍 is simply 'vihāra'; the specific term is not in the Chinese
en_revised: Three or four *li* to the north of the monastery is a *stūpa*, marking the spot where humans and non-humans followed the World-Honored One and stood still as the Tathāgata was proceeding to the country of Kuśinagara (拘尸那國) to enter *parinirvāṇa*. Not far to the northwest is a *stūpa*, marking the spot where the Buddha last gazed upon the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐城). Not far to its south is a vihāra (精舍), with a *stūpa* built in front, marking the site of the Āmrapālī-vana (菴沒羅女園) which she held and offered to the Buddha. Beside the Āmrapālī-vana is a *stūpa*, marking the place where the Tathāgata announced his *nirvāṇa*. Formerly, the Buddha was here and said to Ānanda, "Those who have attained the four bases of psychic power (*catvāraḥ ṛddhi-pādāḥ*) are able to remain for an aeon. The Tathāgata now, how long shall he remain?" In this way he asked three times, but Ānanda did not respond, for he was deluded by the heavenly Māra. Ānanda rose from his seat and went into the forest to meditate in silence. At that time, Māra came to request the Buddha, saying, "The Tathāgata has been in the world teaching and transforming for a long time; those who have been saved from transmigration are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The joy of extinction—now is the time for it." The World-Honored One placed a small amount of soil on his fingernail and said to Māra, "Is the soil of the earth more, or is the soil on my fingernail more?" He replied, "The soil of the earth is more." The Buddha said, "Those whom I have saved are like the soil on my fingernail, while those who have not been saved are like the soil of the great earth. Three months from now, I shall enter *nirvāṇa*." Hearing this, Māra was joyful and withdrew. Ānanda suddenly had a strange dream while in the woods and came to report it to the Buddha, saying: "While I was in the woods, I dreamed of a great tree with luxuriant branches and leaves and dense shade; a violent wind suddenly arose and scattered it until nothing remained. Could it be that the World-Honored One is about to enter extinction? My heart is filled with fear, so I have come to ask." The Buddha told Ānanda: "I told you before that you were obscured by Māra and did not request me to remain at the proper time. The Demon King urged me to enter *nirvāṇa* early, and I have already granted him the date; this dream is the sign of that."  Not far from the place where he announced the time of his *nirvāṇa* is a *stūpa* (窣堵波), which is the place where the thousand sons saw their parents. Long ago, there was a *ṛṣi* (仙人) living in seclusion in a rocky valley. In the second month of spring, while he was bathing in a clear stream, a doe followed him to drink and was moved to give birth to a girl. Her appearance was superior to others, but her feet resembled those of a deer. The *ṛṣi* saw her, took her in, and raised her. Later, he ordered her to seek fire. When she reached the hermitage of another *ṛṣi*, lotus flowers appeared in the tracks where her feet stepped. That *ṛṣi* saw this and, deeply amazed, ordered her to walk around his hermitage before she could obtain the fire. The deer-girl followed his instructions, obtained the fire, and returned.  At that time, King Brahmadatta (梵豫王) was hunting and saw the flowers. He followed the tracks to search for their source, was delighted by their strangeness, and took her back with him in his carriage. A physiognomist predicted that she would give birth to a thousand sons. The other wives heard of this and all began to plot against her. When the months and days were full, she gave birth to a single lotus flower. The flower had a thousand petals, and on each petal sat a son. The other wives slandered her, all claiming it was an inauspicious omen, and threw them into the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) river, where they drifted away with the waves. King Ujjayana (烏耆延王) was sightseeing in the lower reaches of the river when he saw a yellow cloud-like canopy floating on the waves; he took it and opened it to find a thousand sons, whom he nursed and raised until they grew up to possess great strength. Relying on his thousand sons, he expanded his territory in all directions, and riding on the momentum of his military victories, he was about to invade this country. At that time, King Brahmadatta (梵豫王) heard of this and was filled with great fear; his military strength was no match for them, and he could think of no solution. At that moment, the Deer Woman (鹿女) knew in her heart that they were her sons, so she said to the King: "Now that the invaders are at our borders and the people are divided, I, your humble servant, in my simple loyalty, can defeat the powerful enemy." The King did not believe her and remained deeply worried and afraid. The Deer Woman then ascended the city tower to await the arrival of the invaders. The thousand sons led their troops and completely surrounded the city, whereupon the Deer Woman called out to them, "Do not commit such a rebellious act! I am your mother, and you are my sons." The thousand sons replied, "What is this absurd talk?" The Deer Woman pressed her two breasts with her hands, and the milk flowed out in a thousand streams; moved by their natural bond, the milk entered each of their mouths. Thereupon, they took off their armor and returned to their lineage, released their weapons and returned to their kin; the two countries rejoiced together, and the common people were at peace. Not far from where the thousand sons returned to their lineage is a stūpa (窣堵波), which marks the old site where the Tathāgata (如來) once walked. He pointed it out to the assembly and said, "In the past, I returned to my lineage here and saw my relatives. If you wish to know who the thousand sons are, they are the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa (賢劫)." To the east of the place where he narrated his former lives, there is an old foundation upon which a stūpa (窣堵波) is built. It occasionally glows with light, and prayers offered there are sometimes granted; these are the remains of the multi-storied lecture hall where the Tathāgata (如來) preached the *Samantamukha-dhāraṇī* (普門陀羅尼) and other sūtras. Not far from the side of the lecture hall is a stūpa containing the relics of half of Ānanda’s body. Not far from here are several hundred stūpas, and though one might wish to determine their exact number, it has never been known; this is the place where a thousand Pratyekabuddhas (獨覺) entered into extinction (寂滅). Within and surrounding the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐), there are numerous sacred sites, which are difficult to enumerate in full. The old ruins at these scenic and strategic locations stand as thick as fish scales, but as the years have suddenly changed and the seasons have rapidly shifted, the forests have been destroyed and the ponds have dried up; only decayed stumps and remaining traces are left to be examined in detail.

issues: 'to the northeast of the Duyu (Fisherman) country' → 度漁人東北 'northeast of the place where the fishermen were converted' (Mizutani: 度漁人[窣堵波]より)
en_revised: Traveling more than one hundred *li* to the northeast of the place where the fishermen were converted, to the west of an old city, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), over one hundred feet high. It is the place where the Buddha in the past dwelt for six months, preaching the Dharma to save various gods and humans. One hundred forty or fifty paces to the north of this is a small stūpa where the Tathāgata in the past established the precepts for the bhikṣus. Not far to the west of this is a stūpa containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata. At this place, in the past, people from near and far towns would gather together, burning incense, scattering flowers, and keeping lamps and torches burning without interruption.
